<reason>B wins the unresolved clash between comparative parity and preserving usable mobility. It explains why distributed accessible capacity requires additional investment and offers enforceable coverage and maximum-wait obligations as an alternative. A establishes that unequal waits are harmful, but sharing costs does not answer whether wheelchair users should lose already-accessible evening journeys to narrow pickup gaps. A repeatedly substitutes an inaccessible-service example for that harder case and ultimately denies a tradeoff its own answer acknowledged. Its nonexistent reference IDs are a secondary execution flaw.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B directly turns A’s proposal to share reductions in delay and coverage: spreading a cut does not restore the lost journey, and slowing ordinary service can narrow the gap without improving wheelchair pickups. A’s closing does not resolve either objection.</best_rebuttal>
